title: angelos
summary: angelos is a set of instructions that gives Claude expert ways of working. When you ask for something, the skill for that verb reads the ask and opens only the files that job needs, and those files pull their standards from one shared library. The map shows the nine skills (think, build, review, write…), the branches each can open, and the shared knowledge they read.

service.describe: a verb you call, like review or write

route.describe: reads the ask and opens one branch

folder.describe: branches grouped by what they make or judge

module.describe: does one kind of work for its skill

file.describe: a detail or standard, read only when named

data.describe: pulls a standard from shared knowledge when the work needs it

call.describe: passes the work to another skill, or opens a detail file

tours.title: How angelos is wired
tours.question: What are the parts, and how does a request reach the right one?

steps.title: One router per verb
steps.body: Each of the nine skills is a SKILL.md router. It reads the ask, matches one routing row, and that row names the exact files to open. Nothing else is loaded.

simple.title: One cook per kind of dish
simple.body: angelos is like a kitchen with nine cooks, one per kind of job: one thinks, one builds, one reviews, one writes. Each cook first reads your order, then picks the one recipe it needs. That way nobody reads the whole cookbook for a single dish.

steps.title: Branches do the work
steps.body: A matched row opens one branch under skills/<verb>/branches. Review groups its branches by what is judged: code, design, document, plus concerns that stack on any of them.

simple.title: Each cook has a shelf of recipes
simple.body: These smaller boxes are the recipes on the review cook's shelf. Some are for checking code, some for designs, some for documents. The cook only takes down the one that matches your order.

steps.title: Shared knowledge
steps.body: Standards live once under shared/<domain>, as leaves with no index file. A router or branch names the leaves it reads, so the same standard serves the verb that writes and the verb that judges.

simple.title: One rulebook for the whole kitchen
simple.body: This side is the kitchen's rulebook: how clean code should look, how to write good text, what makes a design work. Every cook reads the same pages, so the rules never disagree.

steps.title: A worked path
steps.body: Review on a diff spawns reviewer prompts from shared/code-reviewers, one per failure class. Pick a skill in the filter bar to see only its flow and everything it reads.

simple.title: Watch one order go through
simple.body: Here the review cook is checking some code. It hands the work to a few specialist tasters, each looking for one kind of problem. Try the filter at the top to follow any other cook.

simple.question: Think of a restaurant kitchen. Who does what, and how does an order reach the right cook?

tours.title: Follow a review of a pull request
tours.question: What happens when you ask review to look at a PR?

steps.title: The router matches a change set
steps.body: Review reads the target before it routes: the argument first, then the conversation, then the working tree. A PR number matches the change set row, and that row names every file the run opens.

simple.title: First, read the order carefully
simple.body: Before doing anything, the review cook works out what you gave it: a link to your changes, something you said, or files on your computer. That tells it which recipe to pick.

steps.title: Two branches share the work
steps.body: pr runs the review of the change; code-bugs runs the bug engine over the whole diff. The seventeen flag design scan stays out unless the ask is also about code design.

simple.title: Two recipes split the job
simple.body: One recipe reads your whole change like a careful editor. The other hunts only for bugs, the things that would break. Using both means nothing important gets skipped.

steps.title: Review pulls from the whole shared library
steps.body: Each line leaving review is a standard it can open, across 31 shared domains: code design, security, copy, motion and more. A run opens only what its matched row names. The next steps zoom into the groups a PR review always pulls.

simple.title: The cook can open any page of the rulebook
simple.body: Every line leaving the review cook points to a page it may read: rules for code, safety, writing, design and more. For one order it opens only the pages that order needs. Next we look at the pages every code review uses.

steps.title: Of those, the reviewers are picked by what the diff touches
steps.body: code-reviewers holds one prompt per failure class. Five run on any code. Adversarial joins at 50 changed lines or on auth and payments; api-contract, reliability and data-migrations join by the files touched. Skipping one is allowed only if the report says so.

simple.title: Of those, the tasters are chosen by what you cooked
simple.body: One section of the rulebook is a set of specialist tasters, each looking for one kind of problem. A handful of them always check code. Extra ones join when the change is big or touches risky things like logins or payments, the way a food inspector comes in for raw fish.

steps.title: Every review is held to the anti-sycophancy rules
steps.body: artifacts and claims load on every review row: the run judges the thing, not the author, and does not soften what it found.

simple.title: Honest feedback, always
simple.body: Every review follows a rule: judge the dish, not the cook, and never soften bad news to be nice. These two pages hold that rule.

steps.title: The report shows what ran
steps.body: Severity ranks the findings. The report names every branch, file and reviewer it used or skipped, so a clean pass can be told apart from one that never looked. The map is filtered to review, so everything it can read is still on screen.

simple.title: The receipt shows what was checked
simple.body: The final report lists every problem, worst first, and every check that ran or was skipped. So "no problems found" can never secretly mean "nobody looked".

simple.question: You ask the reviewer to check your changes. What happens, step by step?

tours.title: One standard, two verbs
tours.question: How do the skill that makes a thing and the skill that judges it stay consistent?

steps.title: Knowledge lives once, under shared
steps.body: A branch is procedure: how the work gets done, in what order. What counts as good lives in shared/<domain> as plain leaves, with no index file.

simple.title: The rules live in one place
simple.body: Recipes say how to do the work, step by step. What counts as good lives separately, in this shared rulebook, so it is written down only once.

steps.title: Build writes against code-design
steps.body: When build writes code, its routing names the code-design leaves to open: depth, information hiding, the red flags.

simple.title: The cook follows the rulebook
simple.body: When the build cook writes code, it opens these pages on good code first, the way a chef checks the house standards before plating.

steps.title: Review judges against the same files
steps.body: Review opens those same leaves to judge the result. Nothing is restated in either skill, so the bar cannot drift between making and judging.

simple.title: The critic uses the same rulebook
simple.body: When the review cook judges that code, it opens the very same pages. Maker and judge can never drift apart, because they read one source.

steps.title: Copy follows the same rule
steps.body: content-style is read by build for the strings it writes, by write for the copy it drafts, and by review to judge both.

simple.title: Words work the same way
simple.body: The pages about good writing are read by the cook who builds screens, the one who writes text, and the one who reviews both.

steps.title: Pick a domain to see who reads it
steps.body: The panel lists every skill that reads a domain. Try code-design, then any other domain in the shared lane.

simple.title: Your turn: pick a page
simple.body: The panel on the right shows every cook who reads this part of the rulebook. Click any other part on that side to see who uses it.

simple.question: How do the cook who makes a dish and the critic who tastes it agree on what good means?

tours.title: Adding a branch or a standard
tours.question: Where does a change go, and what has to move with it?

steps.title: A branch exists because a router row names it
steps.body: A file earns its place in skills/<verb>/branches only when a row in SKILL.md opens it. A file no row names is a section of the branch that uses it.

simple.title: A recipe only counts if a cook asks for it
simple.body: A new recipe goes on a cook's shelf only when that cook's order list points to it. A recipe nobody points to is just part of another one.

steps.title: A branch is procedure, never knowledge
steps.body: Every branch has the same shape: Scope, Phases, Report, After. It never loads another branch and never repeats what the router already did.

simple.title: Recipes are steps, not rules
simple.body: Every recipe has the same parts: what it covers, the steps, what it reports, what comes after. It never repeats the rulebook and never calls another recipe.

steps.title: A new standard is a leaf in a domain
steps.body: Knowledge goes into shared/<domain> as one leaf, and the domain is described in docs/shared-domains.md, since the architecture allows no index files.

simple.title: New rules go in the rulebook
simple.body: A new rule becomes one new page in the right section of the shared rulebook, The sections have no table of contents inside them, so each one is described in a single guide instead.

steps.title: Then every consumer names it
steps.body: Each verb that needs the leaf names it in its own routing row. scripts/validate-architecture.sh fails a leaf that no skill names, so an unwired standard is a bug, not a reserve.

simple.title: Then tell every cook who needs it
simple.body: Each cook that should follow the new rule has to point to it. A check fails if a page exists that no cook reads, so a forgotten rule shows up as an error.

simple.question: You want to add something new. Where does it go, and what else has to change?
